as_told: A young woman always cuts both ends off the pot roast (or ham) before she puts it in the pan. When her husband asks why, she says her mother always did it. Her mother says the same about the grandmother. The grandmother explains that her own pan was too small for a whole roast.
lesson: People keep doing things the way they were taught without knowing why, even after the original reason is gone.
what_happened: No real family or event is named in any telling I found. The earliest telling I found is in That Reminds Me (1956), a book of anecdotes for speakers compiled by William F. Weiherman and published by Concordia Publishing House in St. Louis. There a new husband watches his wife cut off part of a ham before it goes in the oven, and someone explains, "Oh, I always did that because my pan was too small" (the search snippet does not show who says it); the item ends with the moral "Never follow custom blindly!" and is followed by a joke about a bride. Later tellings, from 1976 on, add a third generation and change ham to roast.
false_part: The story is a stock humorous anecdote with a moral, not a report of something that happened to real people.

earliest_telling.where: That Reminds Me (St. Louis: Concordia Publishing House, 1956), a book of anecdotes for speakers
earliest_telling.quote: husband  watched  his  wife  prepare  her  first  {{{ham}}} for  the  oven,  and  noticed  that  she  cut  off

original.what: The same 1956 telling: the moral printed at its end (Open Library search snippet)

lesson_verdict.why: Experiments on overimitation show that children who watch an adult use an object copy the adult's unnecessary actions and keep doing so even when warned. They treat the steps as necessary because someone they trust did them.

source.what: Lyons, Young and Keil, The hidden structure of overimitation, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 104(50):19751-19756 (2007), PubMed Central full text
source.quote: children who observe an adult inefficiently operating a novel object frequently engage in what we term overimitation , persistently reproducing the adult's unnecessary actions

search_steps: Open Library full-text search for "cut off the ends" ham pan mother and "cut the ends off" roast pan grandmother: no hits.
Open Library search for "ends off the ham": earliest hit 1980 (Working Couples).

Open Library search for "ends of the ham" "too small": earliest hits are Adelaide Bry's book on est (1976), where the story is told in est training; Daily Bread (1977); and Joseph Boskin, Humor and Social Change in Twentieth-Century America (1979), a book about humor.
Open Library search for "cut off the end of the ham": Zig Ziglar, See You at the Top (1977) and later sales and religious books.

Open Library search for ham "pan was too small": earliest real telling is Weiherman, That Reminds Me (1956; Library of Congress number 55-12194, reissued 1959). Earlier hits (1922, 1935) are about ice pans, not cooking.
Open Library search for ham "pan was too short": Linda Clark, Stay Young Longer (1961). A hit dated 1955 (The Fix) is a modern book with a wrong date.
Open Library search for roast "pan was too small" and "pot roast" ends "too small" grandmother: the roast version appears from 1981 on.
Open Library search for "Never follow custom blindly": confirms the moral at the end of the 1956 item and that the next item is a joke beginning "Bride:".

archive.org metadata for lccn_55012194: That reminds me, compiled by William F. Weiherman, Concordia Publishing House, 1956, subjects Speeches, Anecdotes, Aphorisms. Its full text is lending-only (HTTP 401), so quotes come from Open Library search snippets, not the full text. This bends rule 7.
Web search for origins (USC folklore archive, Snopes, blogs) used only as leads: they record many variants and give no dated source earlier than the books above.
Google Books search was refused with HTTP 429; I did not retry.
No named teller and no correction were found.
confidence_note: A Usenet or newspaper telling earlier than 1956 may exist. The class rests on the earliest telling being an anonymous humorous anecdote with a moral in a speakers' book; no record names a real family.
